The Night Train West

There is a particular kind of waiting that belongs only to night stations, and I had arrived early enough that evening to learn all its varieties. The rain had begun an hour before sunset over Madrid, a thin, needling rain that did not so much fall as hang in the air, silvering the iron ribs of the departures canopy and turning the stone of Chamartin to a dark, polished color. I was too early for the ten o'clock train to Santiago, and so I walked the length of the concourse twice, once with my suitcase and once without it, watching the great board flicker and reset itself, watching people practice the small rituals that make waiting bearable. A man in a suit too warm for October checked his phone, then his watch, then his phone again, as if one of them might finally offer news the other had missed. A woman bought a coffee she clearly did not want and held it for warmth, then left it untouched on a bench. The pigeons, who should have been on the square outside, had found their way inside and were walking the tiles with the slow, offended dignity of pigeons everywhere, inspecting crumbs that did not exist. I bought a newspaper I did not read, a bottle of water I did not need, and a paperback I did not intend to open, simply to have something to carry that was not regret. When the platform was finally announced, we all moved at once, a sudden, polite migration, and the train was there, long and dark and breathing faintly, as if it had been waiting for us longer than we had been waiting for it.

My compartment was a couchette for four, though only three of us would sleep in it that night, a fact I learned only later when the conductor made his quiet, amused inspection and passed on without comment. The interior smelled of other people's journeys layered over one another: boiled coffee from a thermos, oranges, a faint sweetness of eucalyptus cough drops, the rubber and warm metal smell that is the soul of every train in Europe. I had the lower bunk by the window, which is to say I had the best seat in the world for a man who does not intend to sleep very much. I put my bag on the luggage rack, shook the rain from my coat, and sat down with the particular sense of relief that comes from a journey at last being underway after weeks of imagining it. The platform lights began to slide past, first slowly, then with a kind of gathering haste, and Madrid performed its nightly trick of dissolving from a capital city into a scattering of suburbs, into vineyards and dark fields, into nothing at all. The rhythm established itself almost at once, that low, double thump of wheels over joints, and I felt my shoulders drop an inch, which is the body's way of saying it trusts what the mind is still only hoping.

Opposite me, by the time we had cleared the ring road, sat an old woman I would come to think of as Carmen, though she never told me her name and I never asked. She had a shopping trolley folded up against her knees, a plastic bag of clementines, and a rosary wrapped around her wrist like a bracelet. She ate one clementine with great deliberation, peeling it in a perfect spiral, and offered the next segment to me with a gesture so natural it would have been rude to refuse. She was going, she said, to see her grandson who had taken a job in A Coruña, a job she described in terms so vague they might have been any job at all, and she was going at night because the day train, with its bright lights and its announcement of every station in a female voice, left her feeling exposed, somehow, as if everyone could see that she was traveling alone. At night, she said, you are just another person trying to sleep. The train rocked us both in the same direction, and we spoke in the half-whisper that trains impose, the kind of conversation that is not really meant to be heard even by the participants, made up of small courtesies and larger confessions delivered with the safety of not quite being said. She told me she had not slept properly since her husband died, but that trains helped. I believed her completely.

I have always been fascinated by the west, not as a destination but as a direction of the soul. West is where the light goes, everyone learns that as a child, watching the sun perform its slow vanishing act from a bedroom window while the sky turned first gold, then rose, then violet, then a blue so deep it seemed to have weight. West is the direction of returning, of going home at the end of a long day, of the long walk back across a field when the work is done. West is also the direction of the unknown for those of us who have lived in the east of things, in eastern cities and eastern habits of mind, where the map is always pulling your eyes toward the center, toward the capital, toward the place where decisions are made. To travel west at night is to travel in the opposite direction of power. You are leaving the place where the clocks are set, leaving the ministries and the newspapers and the headquarters, and you are going toward the margin, toward the coast, toward the place where the land gives up and the sea begins. It is a modest rebellion, taking a train in that direction, and like most modest rebellions it changes nothing and everything.

The conductor came through at half past eleven, punching tickets with a click that sounded, to my tired ears, like a tiny typewriter, like a poem being written in braille. He was a man of about my age, or perhaps older, with the careful, economical movements of someone who has done the same walk ten thousand times and has learned to waste no motion on it. He asked after Carmen's grandson, by which I understood he knew her, or knew her type, which on this route amounted to the same thing. He checked my ticket, nodded toward the window where the darkness was now absolute except for the occasional farmhouse light, and said simply, "A Coruna by morning, eh?" It was not a question. Night trains have their own small society, and the conductor is its mayor and its priest and its night watchman all at once. He knows who will wake at dawn and who must be allowed to sleep through Santiago, who will want coffee and who will want to be left alone with their grief. He disappears into the corridor, and his absence is as much a part of the train's rhythm as his presence. I watched his shadow pass the frosted glass of the compartment door, and then I was alone again with the sound of the rails and the woman opposite me, who had begun, very quietly, to sleep.

There is a moment, somewhere after midnight, when a night train passes through a place you will later try to name and fail. The train slows for a station you do not recognize, the platform is empty except for a single figure under a single lamp, perhaps waiting for a connection that no longer exists, and then the train accelerates again into the dark. That night we slowed, I think, for Talavera, or perhaps for a smaller place whose name never reached me, and the slowing woke Carmen for an instant. She opened her eyes, looked out at the empty platform, and murmured something I could not hear, perhaps a prayer, perhaps a name. The town, if it was a town, had the hushed quality of places that have been awake longer than they meant to be. I thought of all the stationmasters who have ever stood on platforms like that one, in rain much like ours, holding a lamp or a lantern or now just standing there, waiting for a train that might be carrying one person who matters to them. We are all waiting for someone to arrive by train, even if we pretend we are only traveling ourselves. The train passed on, and the platform and its solitary figure were swallowed by the night again, as if they had been a scene in a play that we had interrupted by passing through.

I did not sleep, or rather I slept in the way one sleeps on trains, which is to say I surrendered to a series of brief, porous unconsciousnesses from which I woke with my heart beating faster than the wheels. Between those brief descents, I watched the window. A train window at night is a strange mirror. It shows you the interior of the compartment superimposed on the landscape rushing past, so that your own face floats ghostlike over fields and hills, and the lights of the compartment cast a warm amber rectangle onto the trees. It is like watching two films at once, one of them about you, the other about the world you are leaving behind. At some point the moon rose, a thin crescent that seemed to follow us for miles, as if it too were a passenger who had boarded without a ticket. I thought about how many people the moon has watched traveling in exactly this way, over centuries, on horses, on foot, on bicycles, on trains that burned coal and trains that burned diesel and now trains that burn electricity generated by water falling somewhere in the mountains I could not see. The moon does not judge our conveyances. It simply keeps its faint light on us, a reminder that we are small and moving and brief.

When I woke properly, or as properly as one wakes at three in the morning in a moving train, the third passenger was there. He had boarded, I think, at Avila, or perhaps he had been there all along, wrapped in a blanket I had not noticed. He was a young man, perhaps twenty-five, with a backpack at his feet and a book face-down on his chest, open to a page he was not reading. He sat up when I sat up, and we nodded at each other with the instant, wordless solidarity of people who are awake when they could be sleeping. He told me, without my asking, that he was an Argentine who had come to Spain to walk the Camino Frances, but had run out of time and money in equal measure, and so he was taking the train the rest of the way to Santiago, where he would get his compostela, the certificate of completion, which he admitted with a grin was a lie he planned to tell his mother. I told him, as I would have told anyone at three in the morning, that the lie was the truest part of the story, that everyone who walks to Santiago walks it in their own way, and that the certificate, if it came, would be a souvenir of a journey that had already happened inside him. He laughed, and the sound was so young and so unguarded that Carmen opened one eye, smiled, and closed it again.

We talked, in that low register, about the things that young men who have been walking alone for a month tend to talk about when they finally have an audience. He told me about the blisters, about the kindness of strangers who offered plums and advice in equal, unsolicited measure, about the German woman of sixty who walked faster than anyone he had ever met and never stopped singing, about the night he had slept in a field outside a village because the albergue was full and the stars had been so bright he had felt rude to go indoors. He told me about the moment, somewhere on the meseta, when the wind had blown so steadily for so long that he had begun to feel himself being gently taken apart and reassembled in a different order. I told him about my own long walk, which had been not a walk at all but a series of night trains and rented rooms and notebooks, and how I had come to believe that the Camino, in its oldest sense, is simply any road that makes you honest. He considered this, as young men do, with his whole face, and then said, "My mother will like that." Outside, the landscape had changed. The hard, yellow plains of Castile had given way to a softer, greener darkness, the darkness of Galicia, where the rain, when it comes, comes more often and more gently, and where everything is older and damper and somehow more alive.

I have always thought that aqueducts are the saddest of monuments, because they were built to carry water to a city, and most of them now carry nothing, and the cities they served have grown so large and so changed that the water would be a stranger to them now. That night, as we passed somewhere near Segovia, though I could not see it, I thought of the arches standing in the dark, holding up nothing, patient as saints. Trains pass through history without stopping for it. We do not get off to look at the castle, or the cathedral, or the battlefield. We are carried through a landscape that has been fought over and prayed over and farmed and abandoned and reclaimed, and we sleep through most of it, which is perhaps the most honest way to travel through history. We cannot look at everything. We can only be carried, and trust that the land, in its wisdom, will go on being there whether we see it or not. At dawn, when we finally began to see the hills of Galicia emerge from the mist, I felt a sudden, irrational gratitude for all the places I had slept through, for the faith that the train, like time itself, would deliver me to the far end without requiring me to earn it by staying awake.

By the time the sky in the east began its slow, complicated change of color, Carmen was awake and dressed, her trolley unfolded, her rosary back on her wrist. She ate the last of her clementines and offered me the peel, which I declined with thanks. The young Argentine had his backpack on his knees, ready to stand the moment the train sighed to a stop. The conductor made his final round, punching, nodding, saying "Santiago, Santiago" in a voice that was both announcement and benediction. The train slowed, and the suburbs of Santiago de Compostela began to appear, first as scattered lights, then as apartment blocks, then as the particular, rain-washed stone of the old town. I watched a woman watering plants on a balcony, a man walking a dog in a coat, a bus pulling away from a stop. Ordinary life, resuming. The train drew into the station with a sigh of brakes and a clatter that sounded, absurdly, like applause. We got off into the damp air of a Galician morning, and the three of us stood on the platform for a moment, united by a night we would never share again, and then we went our separate ways, as travelers do, without exchanging numbers or addresses, because the whole point of a night train is that it creates a brief, perfect community that dissolves on arrival.

Santiago in the morning is a city that seems to have been built for arrivals. The cathedral rises over everything, its towers dripping after the night's rain, its bells beginning their slow, sonorous argument with the sky. Pilgrims gather in the square, some of them weeping, some of them laughing with a wild, tired joy, some of them simply standing still, as if they cannot quite believe that the walking is over. I stood among them, not a pilgrim but a witness, and felt the strange, familiar ache that comes from watching other people complete a journey you have only imagined. The smell of incense drifted from the open doors, mingled with coffee from a hundred cafes and the wet stone smell of the streets. A group of teenagers in matching windbreakers sang, off-key and completely without embarrassment, a song I did not recognize. A man in a wheelchair reached out to touch the facade of the cathedral, and his hand came away wet. I bought coffee and stood under an awning, and I thought about Carmen and the young Argentine, and about how the train had carried us west, all of us, toward the end of the known world, and how none of us, despite our different reasons, had really been going to Santiago at all.

Because the train ends at Santiago, and Santiago is not the end. The end, if you are going west, is Finisterre, the cape that the Romans called the end of the earth, where the lighthouse stands and the Atlantic begins in earnest. I took a bus the next day, a slow, local bus that stopped in every village and smelled of diesel and sea air, and we drove through a landscape that grew greener and wilder with every mile. The road wound through eucalyptus forests that dripped in the sun, past small harbors where fishing boats rocked at their moorings, past fields where cows stood in the rain looking profoundly unbothered. The bus driver knew the road the way the conductor knew the train, by heart and by habit, and he waved at people in doorways and stopped an extra minute for an old man who was walking slowly toward the stop with a stick. I thought about how a community is simply a group of people who agree to stop for each other, and how the night train, for all its speed, had been an act of community too, a rolling village that existed for twelve hours and then vanished.

At Finisterre, the wind is a physical presence. It pushes against you, it finds the gaps in your coat, it makes the sea white at the edges. The lighthouse is not romantic in the way lighthouses are romantic in stories. It is a practical, white, cylindrical building with a red top, standing on a rock that is lashed by waves in winter and visited by tourists in summer. I climbed to the point as far as the path allowed, past the bronze statue of a pilgrim straining against the wind, past the kilometer zero marker where the Camino ends, where pilgrims burn their boots or leave them as offerings, a pile of worn leather that smells of endings. Beyond the path, the Atlantic spread out to the horizon in all directions, a vast, indifferent, magnificent indifference. Ships appeared as tiny specks and disappeared again. The sky was the color of slate and light at once. I stood there for a long time, doing nothing, which is perhaps the most important thing one can do at the end of the earth. I thought about how, for centuries, men believed that beyond this point there was only chaos and monsters. I thought about how wrong we are, so often, about what lies beyond the last known point, and how the sea, that great west, does not contain monsters but only distance, and distance, properly considered, is not a threat but a kind of grace.

I did not take the night train back. I took a daytime train, which is a different country entirely, bright and noisy and full of announcements, and I watched the landscape I had slept through come back to life in full color. The meseta was golden, the mountains were blue, the rivers were silver ribbons. It was beautiful, and it was entirely different from the night journey, and neither was truer than the other. The night train had given me a story that belonged to the dark, to the half-dreams and the quiet confidences and the moon that followed us. The day train gave me a landscape that belonged to the light, to the castles on their hills and the farms in their valleys. I have come to believe that we need both kinds of travel, the one that shows us the world and the one that shows us ourselves in transit between worlds. I still have the ticket stub from that night, folded in a notebook, punched by the conductor with his tiny typewriter. It is not much to look at, a scrap of paper with a date and a route and a hole where the punch fell. But when I find it, I am back in that compartment, listening to the double thump of the wheels, watching the moon follow us west, feeling my shoulders drop an inch as the train, breathing faintly in the dark, carries me, and all of us, toward the end of the earth, where the light goes down and the sea begins and the journey, finally, is over.

I thought about how a community is simply a group of people who agree to stop for each other, and how the night train, for all its speed, had been an act of community too, a rolling village that existed for twelve hours and then vanished.

At Finisterre, the wind is a physical presence. It pushes against you, it finds the gaps in your coat, it makes the sea white at the edges. The lighthouse is not romantic in the way lighthouses are romantic in stories. It is a practical, white, cylindrical building with a red top, standing on a rock that is lashed by waves in winter and visited by tourists in summer. I climbed to the point as far as the path allowed, past the bronze statue of a pilgrim straining against the wind, past the kilometer zero marker where the Camino ends, where pilgrims burn their boots or leave them as offerings, a pile of worn leather that smells of endings. Beyond the path, the Atlantic spread out to the horizon in all directions, a vast, indifferent, magnificent indifference. Ships appeared as tiny specks and disappeared again. The sky was the color of slate and light at once. I stood there for a long time, doing nothing, which is perhaps the most important thing one can do at the end of the earth. I thought about how, for centuries, men believed that beyond this point there was only chaos and monsters. I thought about how wrong we are, so often, about what lies beyond the last known point, and how the sea, that great west, does not contain monsters but only distance, and distance, properly considered, is not a threat but a kind of grace.

I did not take the night train back. I took a daytime train, which is a different country entirely, bright and noisy and full of announcements, and I watched the landscape I had slept through come back to life in full color. The meseta was golden, the mountains were blue, the rivers were silver ribbons. It was beautiful, and it was entirely different from the night journey, and neither was truer than the other. The night train had given me a story that belonged to the dark, to the half-dreams and the quiet confidences and the moon that followed us. The day train gave me a landscape that belonged to the light, to the castles on their hills and the farms in their valleys. I have come to believe that we need both kinds of travel, the one that shows us the world and the one that shows us ourselves in transit between worlds. I still have the ticket stub from that night, folded in a notebook, punched by the conductor with his tiny typewriter. It is not much to look at, a scrap of paper with a date and a route and a hole where the punch fell. But when I find it, I am back in that compartment, listening to the double thump of the wheels, watching the moon follow us west, feeling my shoulders drop an inch as the train, breathing faintly in the dark, carries me, and all of us, toward the end of the earth, where the light goes down and the sea begins and the journey, finally, is over.
